Earning Income and Payroll: Pay calculated as a rate times hours worked
A fixed annual amount divided across pay periods
Premium pay, usually 1.5 times the rate beyond forty hours
Pay calculated as a percentage of sales made
Pay based on the number of units produced
Converting a periodic paycheck into a yearly total
Additional taxable income from customer payments
Earnings where the worker owes both halves of payroll tax
Taxes and Deductions: Income tax
A tax levied on earnings by federal and often state government
Withholding
Tax deducted from each paycheck and sent to the government
Form W-4
The form telling an employer how much tax to withhold
Form W-2
The annual summary of wages and taxes withheld
FICA
The combined Social Security and Medicare payroll tax
Social Security tax rate
6.2 percent of wages paid by the employee
Medicare tax rate
1.45 percent of wages paid by the employee
Marginal tax rate
The rate applied to the last dollar of income earned
Effective tax rate
Total tax divided by total income
Progressive tax brackets
Higher portions of income taxed at higher rates
Standard deduction
A fixed amount subtracted from income before tax
Taxable income
Income remaining after deductions are subtracted
Tax credit versus deduction
A direct reduction of tax owed versus a reduction of taxable income
Tax refund
Money returned when withholding exceeded the tax owed
Sales tax
A percentage added to a purchase price at checkout
Property tax
A tax based on assessed real estate value
Banking and Checking Accounts: Checking account
A deposit account designed for frequent transactions
Savings account
A deposit account that earns interest on the balance
Debit card
A card that draws directly from a checking balance
Direct deposit
Electronic delivery of a paycheck into an account
Account reconciliation
Comparing your register to the bank statement
Outstanding check
A written check the bank has not yet processed
Overdraft
Spending more than the account balance
Overdraft fee
A charge assessed for spending beyond the balance
Available balance
The funds usable right now, excluding pending items
FDIC insurance
Federal protection of deposits up to a stated limit per depositor
Routing number
The nine-digit code identifying a financial institution
Automatic transfer
A scheduled recurring movement of money between accounts
Monthly maintenance fee
A recurring charge some accounts assess
Budgeting: A plan matching expected income to planned spending
A cost that stays the same each month, such as rent
A cost that changes month to month, such as groceries
Optional spending on wants rather than needs
Allocating half to needs, thirty percent to wants, twenty to saving
Assigning every dollar of income a specific job
Income remaining after all planned spending
Spending more than income in a period
Savings covering three to six months of expenses
Money set aside gradually for a known future expense
Recording actual spending to compare against the plan
The typical amount needed to cover basic expenses in an area
What you give up by choosing one purchase over another
Credit and Credit Scores: Credit
The ability to borrow money or buy now and pay later
Credit card
A revolving line of credit with a set limit
Credit limit
The maximum balance a card allows
Annual percentage rate
The yearly cost of borrowing expressed as a percentage
Minimum payment
The smallest payment that avoids a late fee, which maximises interest
Grace period
The window to pay in full without incurring interest
Credit utilization
Balance owed as a percentage of available credit
Credit score
A number, commonly 300 to 850, summarising creditworthiness
Payment history
The largest factor in a credit score
Credit report
The detailed record of borrowing behaviour from a bureau
Hard inquiry
A credit check for a new application that can lower a score
Secured credit card
A card backed by a deposit, used to build credit
Default
Failure to repay a debt as agreed
Identity theft
Someone using your personal information to obtain credit
Loans and Interest: Principal
The original amount borrowed or invested
Simple interest
Interest computed only on the principal
Compound interest
Interest computed on principal plus accumulated interest
Compounding frequency
How often interest is added, such as monthly or daily
Rule of 72
Dividing 72 by the rate to estimate doubling time in years
Amortization
Paying off a loan through scheduled equal payments
Amortization schedule
A table showing interest and principal in each payment
Term of a loan
The length of time over which a loan is repaid
Installment loan
A loan repaid in fixed periodic payments
Total cost of a loan
The sum of all payments, which exceeds the amount borrowed
Down payment
Cash paid upfront that reduces the amount financed
Collateral
An asset pledged that the lender can seize on default
Secured versus unsecured loan
Backed by collateral versus backed only by a promise
Student loan subsidized versus unsubsidized
Interest paid by the government while in school versus accruing
Payday loan
A very short-term loan with extremely high effective interest
Refinancing
Replacing a loan with a new one, usually at a better rate
Investing Basics: Investment
Committing money now expecting future returns
Stock
A share of ownership in a company
Bond
A loan to a company or government paying interest
Dividend
A share of company profit paid to stockholders
Capital gain
Profit from selling an asset above its purchase price
Mutual fund
A professionally managed pool of many securities
Index fund
A fund tracking a market index at low cost
Exchange-traded fund
An index-style fund that trades like a stock
Diversification
Spreading investments to reduce single-asset risk
Risk-return tradeoff
Higher expected returns come with greater risk
Rate of return
Gain or loss expressed as a percentage of the amount invested
Time value of money
A dollar today is worth more than a dollar later
Dollar-cost averaging
Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals
Brokerage account
An account used to buy and sell securities
Volatility
How much an investment's value fluctuates
Inflation risk
The chance returns fail to keep pace with rising prices
Insurance: A contract transferring financial risk to an insurer
The recurring payment made to keep a policy active
The amount you pay before coverage begins
A fixed fee paid for a covered service
The percentage of a covered cost you share after the deductible
The annual cap on what you must pay yourself
A request for payment under an insurance policy
Insurance paying for harm you cause to others
Auto insurance covering damage to your own vehicle
Auto insurance for non-collision damage such as theft
Coverage for personal belongings in a rented home
Coverage for a set period with no cash value
Permanent coverage that builds cash value
Lower premiums but more risk retained by you
Housing and Rent Versus Buy: Mortgage
A long-term loan secured by real estate
Fixed-rate mortgage
A mortgage with an unchanging interest rate
Adjustable-rate mortgage
A mortgage whose rate changes after an initial period
Principal and interest payment
The core portion of a monthly mortgage payment
Escrow
An account holding funds for property taxes and insurance
Private mortgage insurance
Insurance required when a down payment is under twenty percent
Home equity
The portion of a home's value the owner actually owns
Appreciation
An increase in a property's market value
Closing costs
Fees paid at the completion of a real estate purchase
Security deposit
Refundable money a renter provides against damage
Lease
A binding rental contract for a set term
Renter's advantages
Flexibility, lower upfront cost, and no maintenance responsibility
Owner's advantages
Equity building, tax benefits, and stable payments
28 percent rule
A guideline capping housing cost at 28 percent of gross income
Utilities
Recurring service costs such as electricity, water, and internet
Retirement Planning: Retirement
The stage of life when a person stops working for income
401(k) plan
An employer-sponsored retirement account funded by payroll deferral
Employer match
Money an employer contributes alongside your own
Vesting
The schedule on which employer contributions become fully yours
Traditional IRA
An account with tax-deductible contributions taxed at withdrawal
Roth IRA
An account funded with after-tax money that grows tax free
Contribution limit
The annual maximum the law allows into an account
Early withdrawal penalty
An extra tax for taking retirement funds before age 59 and a half
Compounding over time
The reason starting to invest early matters enormously
Pension
A retirement plan promising defined payments from an employer
Social Security retirement benefit
A government payment based on lifetime earnings
Asset allocation
The mix of stocks, bonds, and cash in a portfolio
Target-date fund
A fund that automatically grows more conservative near retirement
Withdrawal rate
The percentage of savings spent each year in retirement
